paragraphs.text: This loose leaf is [Liu Bao](liu-bao:definition), the [dark tea](dark:definition) of [Guangxi](guangxi:where-it-is) in the south of China, made in 1990. The style is named for the town of Liubao in Cangwu County, near Wuzhou, where a warm, wet [subtropical monsoon climate](guangxi:land-and-climate) suits the microbes that shape a dark tea. That is why the trade ties the long, slow ageing of Liu Bao to this land. It was made for a market far from home: Chinese miners and labourers in Malaya and across Southeast Asia drank it, above all in the tin mines, because they believed it eased the heat and damp of their work.

As with every dark tea, the leaf was heaped after it was made so that warmth, moisture and microbes would darken it, and then it was left to age. At thirty-six years it is far past the ten that the trade counts as [aged Liu Bao](liu-bao:age-aged). Over that time, how the tea was stored has shaped it as much as the years have.

brewing.text: Liu Bao takes very hot or boiling water, because its leaf is dense and gives up its depth slowly. Rinse it once or twice and pour the rinse away. Use about 5 to 8 grams to 100 ml, start with steeps of five to fifteen seconds and add a few seconds each round; a good Liu Bao gives ten cups or more.

notice.text: A deep red, thick cup with woody, herbal and betel nut notes; tea several decades old is often described with ginseng and camphor.
